The text layer is two-column; on pages 8 and 9 (Experiment III) it interleaves the two columns line by line, so quotes from that passage are fragments that sit on one layer line. papers.what_it_is: A preliminary experimental study that formulates non-negative matrix factorization as a quartic polynomial (for the Dirac-3 entropy computer) and as a QUBO, and compares Dirac-3 with scikit-learn (real matrices) and with Google CP-SAT (integer matrices) on matrices of at most 4 by 8.

existing.value: The authors state that the Dirac-3 machine can have up to 39 variables for a quartic objective function, which limits the preliminary experiments to 39 variables.
quotes: Dirac-3 machine can have up to 39 variables for a quartic objective function [45]. Therefore, in the preliminary experiments we now describe, we are limited to 39 variables.
existing.certainty_reason: Section IV states the device limit and that all experiments are held to it.
existing.reader_inference: The 39 figure is cited to the vendor spec sheet (reference 45), so it is the vendor's number for the machine as of the paper's date.

existing.note: The paper limits this to Experiment II (rectangular real matrices, two test sets of one hundred cases each). The fusion wins in a majority of cases, but the median improvement is close to zero for test set A and between 70-75% for test set B, and the Dirac-3 output alone was always inferior to scikit-learn. Tables III and IV (anchors only, not quotable) also show the fusion can be much worse in single cases.
existing.value: The authors report that in Experiment II the matrix reconstructed from Dirac-3 output alone was always inferior in relative error to the scikit-learn result, and that the fusion (Dirac-3 output used as the initial factor matrices of scikit-learn) outperformed scikit-learn alone in the majority of cases for both relaxation schedules; the median improvement was between 70-75% for test set B and close to zero for test set A.
existing.anchor: Section IV-B2, p.6-8, Tables I to IV
quotes: was always inferior, in terms of relative error, to that produced with the sklearn approach
Tables I and II show that for the majority of cases, for both relaxation schedules (labeled RS), the fusion approach outperforms the plain sklearn method in terms of relative error.
In fact, while the median improvement for test set B is between 70-75%, the median improvement for test set A is close to zero.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study on generated matrices with a small number of variables.
existing.reader_inference: Table I (test set A) counts, as printed: fusion better 78 and 77, scikit-learn better 22 and 23, for relaxation schedules 1 and 2. Table II (test set B): fusion better 75 and 90, scikit-learn better 25 and 10. I recomputed the one-sided binomial p-values from these counts and they match the paper's. The comparison is Dirac-3 median-energy run fed to scikit-learn against scikit-learn started from its default initialization, so the fusion is a different initialization, not an extra optimization step with equal information.

papers.what_it_is: A simulation study of a Qiskit variational quantum classifier on the Titanic dataset under dataset-level, angle-space and circuit-level noise.

existing.value: The authors report that under ideal execution, with no dataset-level perturbations and no quantum circuit noise, the variational quantum classifier achieved a mean training accuracy of 76.40% and a mean testing accuracy of 76.12%.
quotes: the variational quantum classifier achieved a mean training accuracy of 76.40% and a closely matching mean testing accuracy of 76.12%.
existing.reader_inference: Single Titanic split with fixed seeds and statevector execution; the paper reports no classical-model baseline for comparison.

existing.note: Stored value is right on the numbers and on amplitude damping. The paper limits it: the figures are means over circuit-noise configurations built from depolarizing, amplitude damping, phase damping and their combinations, with a noise-free dataset; the appendix bar labels show single configurations at 38 to 41 percent.
existing.value: The authors report that with the classical dataset noise-free, introducing circuit-level quantum noise (across depolarizing, amplitude damping, phase damping, and their combinations) reduced mean training accuracy from approximately 76% to 38.67% and mean testing accuracy to 39.15%, and that amplitude damping consistently had the most severe impact on both loss convergence and final accuracy.
quotes: Across depolarizing, amplitude damping, phase damping, and their combinations, meant training accuracy collapsed from approximately 76% to 38.67%, while mean testing accuracy droped to 39.15%.
Among the four quantum noise channels, amplitude damping consistently exhibited the most severe impact on both loss convergence and final accuracy.
existing.reader_inference: Appendix accuracy bar labels (Figure 6) read 38 to 41 percent for the noisy configurations; the amplitude-damping-only bar is not distinguishable from the others at that resolution.

existing.note: The abstract states that classical input noise intensifies decoherence effects. Section V.E reports the opposite for the combined runs: accuracy stays at the circuit-noise floor and extra dataset corruption adds negligible degradation. The abstract claim holds only in the paper's 'low-to-moderate circuit noise regimes' wording, for which no separate data is shown.

In Section V.E they report that with dataset-level and circuit noise applied together, mean training and testing accuracies remained near 39%, with additional dataset corruption contributing negligible further degradation once strong quantum noise was present.
quotes: noise in classical input data can significantly intensify the effects of quantum decoherence, resulting in less stable training and noticeably lower classification accuracy.

existing.reader_inference: The abstract claim is not supported by the combined results as reported: Table 2 gives the same 39.15 ± 0.83 for circuit noise only and for dataset plus circuit noise. Each noise strength is fixed, so no low-to-moderate circuit noise regime was varied.

papers.title_in_file: Contextuality and inductive bias in quantum machine learning
papers.what_it_is: A preprint that defines contextuality for multi-task learning models, proves that a noncontextual model class encoding a linear conserved-quantity bias is limited in expressivity, and compares a biased quantum model with classical surrogates on a rock, paper, scissors toy problem.

existing.value: The authors state that contextuality is tied to expressivity: contextual model classes that encode the inductive bias are generally more expressive than their noncontextual counterparts.
